Problem 1Find the least positive integer $n$ that allows the expression $\sum_{i=3}^{n}\dbinom{n}{3}$ to be greater than or equal to $2019$.


Problem 2Compute the number of ways to order the seven integers in the set ${2017, 2017, 2018, 2018, 2018, 2019, 2019}$ where all pairs of adjacent items in the arrangement are relatively prime. Note that items of the same value are considered indistinguishable.


Problem 3Four children and three adults sit around a round table with ten chairs to have a New Years' dinner party. Each person will take exactly one seat. However, Jessica (who is a child) wants to sit at least three chairs away from John (who is also a child) because he always picks his nose. (J1, *empty*, *empty*, J2 is okay, but J1, *empty*, J2 is not an acceptable seating arrangement.) The twins Sam and Joseph (who are children) want to sit together to play the new 2019 edition of Fortnite. The three adults, Mr. Smith, Mrs. Smith, and Grandmother Annie have to sit in a certain order: Mr. Smith first, Mrs. Smith next, and Grandmother Annie last. This order must always be in a clockwise direction. Given that if an arrangement can be formed by rotating another arrangement, they are considered indistinguishable, how many seating arrangements are there for the seven people?


Problem 4Let $N$ be the number of ways to order the digits of the twelve-digit positive integer 201820182019 where no two odd digits are adjacent to each other and that the re-ordering produces another twelve-digit positive integer. Given that digits of the same value are considered indistinguishable, find $\frac{N}{2}$.

topics.title: mathchampion1 Personal Problem Set #6
topics.text:
ProblemWhen the sum $$(1\cdot 2 \cdot 3) + (2\cdot 3 \cdot 4) + (3\cdot 4\cdot 5) + \cdots + (2018 \cdot 2019 \cdot 2020)$$is evaluated, what is the units digit of the result?




This problem is from mathchampion1’s Personal Problem Set handout.



SolutionThis problem is equivalent to evaluating the sum $\pmod{10}.$ Let a multiplication group (e.g. $2 \cdot 3 \cdot 4$) be called a component. It is obvious that every component is a multiple of $2$. In addition, for any given $5$ components, three of them will be divisible by $5$ (proving this is left as an exercise to the reader) and thus by $10.$ This is very useful, since if the component is a multiple of $10,$ then the units digit of it will be $0$ and it will not contribute to the units digit of the sum. We now have to evaluate the units digits of the components that are not divisible by $5$ (e.g. $2 \cdot 3 \cdot 4 \equiv 4 \pmod{10}$).



Let $n$ be a multiple of $5.$ The two next components that are not multiples of $5$ are $(n+1)(n+2)(n+3)$ and $(n+2)(n+3)(n+4).$ If we evaluate these mod 5, we find that the first evaluates to $1 \pmod 5$ and the second evaluates to $4 \pmod 5.$ Thus their sum is $0 \pmod 5.$ Hence in any group of $5$ components, the sum will always be $0 \pmod 5. $ Thus from $n=1$ to $n=2015,$ the units digits of these components is $0.$ This leaves $n=2016 \to n=2018.$ $n=2016$ evaluates to $1 \pmod 5$, $n = 2017$ evaluates to $4 \pmod{5},$ and $n=2018$ evaluates to $0 \pmod{5}.$ Hence the units digit of the overall sum is $\boxed{0}.$

topics.title: Hill Cipher
topics.text:
NikoIsLife wants to encrypt a message using Hill Cipher. He/she does this by randomly generating a $2\times2$ matrix, where each of the terms are integers from $0$ to $25$.



However, doing this method has some problems. To do Hill Cipher, the matrix needs to be invertible. A matrix $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$ is invertible, if and only if $ad-bc$ is relatively prime to $26$.



For example, $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&25\end{pmatrix}$ is an invertible matrix, because $1\cdot25-0\cdot0=25$ is relatively prime to $26$.



The matrix $\begin{pmatrix}6&9\\21&12\end{pmatrix}$ is not invertible, because $6\cdot12-9\cdot21=-117$ is not relatively prime to $26$.



What is the probability that NikoIsLife generates a $2\times2$ matrix that is not invertible?



Bonus QuestionNikoIsLife wants to be more secure. So instead of using a $2\times2$ matrix, NikoIsLife uses an $n\times n$ matrix. An $n\times n$ matrix is said to be invertible if its determinant is relatively prime to $26$.



What is the probability that NikoIsLife generates an $n\times n$ matrix that is not invertible?

To win this competition, you'll have to have the most points in the competition. These problems will be derived from $\text{MATHCOUNTS}$ and the $\text{AMC 8}$. Each question has a different point number. The one who gets the most points after a 3-hour period wins. This competition will start at $10:00\text{ AM(EST)}$ and last until $1:00\text{ PM(EST)}$.

P1(2 points)In trapezoid $ABCD$, the sides $AB$ and $CD$ are equal. The perimeter of $ABCD$ is



IMAGE

$\text{(A)}\ 27 \qquad \text{(B)}\ 30 \qquad \text{(C)}\ 32 \qquad \text{(D)}\ 34 \qquad \text{(E)}\ 48$


P2(5 points)Points $B$, $D$, and $J$ are midpoints of the sides of right triangle $ACG$. Points $K$, $E$, $I$ are midpoints of the sides of triangle $JDG$, etc. If the dividing and shading process is done 100 times (the first three are shown) and $AC=CG=6$, then the total area of the shaded triangles is nearest



IMAGE

$\text{(A)}\ 6 \qquad \text{(B)}\ 7 \qquad \text{(C)}\ 8 \qquad \text{(D)}\ 9 \qquad \text{(E)}\ 10$


P3(4 points)At Central Middle School the 108 students who take the AMC 8 meet in the evening to talk about problems and eat an average of two cookies apiece. Walter and Gretel are baking Bonnie's Best Bar Cookies this year. Their recipe, which makes a pan of 15 cookies, lists this items: $1\frac{1}{2}$ cups of flour, $2$ eggs, $3$ tablespoons butter, $\frac{3}{4}$ cups sugar, and $1$ package of chocolate drops. They will make only full recipes, not partial recipes.



Walter can buy eggs by the half-dozen. How many half-dozens should he buy to make enough cookies? (Some eggs and some cookies may be left over.)



$\text{(A)}\ 1 \qquad \text{(B)}\ 2 \qquad \text{(C)}\ 5 \qquad \text{(D)}\ 7 \qquad \text{(E)}\ 15$

topics.title: k Number Theory Marathon
topics.text:
InspirationJSGandora's Beginning Algebra Marathon




I would like to start a Number Theory Marathon. Here are the rules:



[list]

[*]Please number your problems and solutions so that people will know which problem/solution you are referring to, and use the "hide" tags for your problems and solutions, like this:

[code]Problem/Solution NumberProblem/Solution
[/code]

[*]I will post the first problem. Someone else can post a full solution to my problem (remember to use the "hide" tags and numbering) in addition to posting a new problem. If you don't have a new problem, you can always use AoPS or Google, but remember to cite your source

[*]Why is it important to use hide tags and numberings for your problems and solutions?You should use the "hide" tags so that people won't have to have the solutions staring at them right in the face.  When the solution is easily accessible, people will have a tendency to look at it right away if they can't do the problem on the first try, and if you do that, you aren't learning at all.



Additionally, you should also number your problems so that referencing different problems can be much less problematic.


[*]Above all, remember the level of this marathon, this is an Intermediate Number Theory Marathon. Just remember to keep the problems at a relatively middle school level, but still challenge the AoPS community.[/list]

P1Find the total number of whole number factors of $400$.

topics.title: Self-Referential Marathon!
topics.text:
Hi, everyone!



I want to start a new marathon that is going to be very unique. In this, you basically post a problem that references its own answer in the problem statement.



For (a boring) example, "Provided that it is positive, what is the square of the answer to this problem?"

Answer: 1

Details: If the answer to the problem is $x$, then $x=x^2 \implies x(x-1)=0$, so $x=0$ or $x=1$, but because it's positive, $x=\boxed{1}$.



Please use the traditional problem/answer format!

topics.title: Xmas math
topics.text:
Merry Christmas everyone!

For everyone who is browsing these forums today, here are (pretty easy) problems to keep you occupied.

Note: $a_n$ refers to the answer for problem n.

For example:

Problem 22: What is 1+1?

Problem 23: What is $a_{22}$+3?

The answer to problem 23 would be 5.



problem1Santa has 6 dolls and 6 trucks to hand out to 3 brother and one sister. Given that each kids must receive an equal number of toys to prevent toddler tantrums, in how many ways can Santa place the toys in the stockings?


problem2It's New Year's Eve and I just realized that I messed up the batch of cookies I was supposed to make. Oh no! I realize that if I don't eat any cookies, then each of my 6 guests will get an equal number of cookies with none left over. However, if I also get cookies and each of us (7 people) eat an equal number, then there will be three cookies left. What is the least number of cookies I could have baked?


problem3Santa's elves are having a food fight instead of wrapping presents, and all 4 elves turn to another elf randomly and throw their cupcake. Let the probability that two elves throw cupcakes at each other be $\frac{m}{n}$. Find m+n.


problem4All of Ms. Bindergarten's (many) students line up in rows every day with a different number of students in each row every day. On day 1, there are $a_1$ students in a row. On day 2, there are $a_2$ students in a row. If Ms. Bindergarten has the least number of students needed to arrange them with $a_1$ and $a_2$ students in a row on Day 1 and 2 respectively, for how many days can she continue to arrange them with a new number in each row before she is forced to repeat an arrangement?


problem5Dasher, Dancer, and Prancer are doing laps on a circular track to prepare for their big reindeer race. Dasher take $a_1$ seconds for a lap, Dancer takes $a_4$ seconds for a lap, and Prancer takes $a_2$ seconds for a lap. After how many seconds will all three reindeer meet again?


problem6Ebenezer Scrooge, after his new-found altruism, is excited to donate money to homeless people outside the church. However, he has a problem: He is going donate all the money that he takes, but he wants to make sure each person gets an equal amount and he doesn't know how many people there will be. Assuming that he has less than 1000  dollars in his bank account, how many dollars should he take to maximize his chance of being able to donate an equal amount to all the homeless people that show up?




Hide your answers and have fun!



Edit: Problem 4 didn't make sense before, but it has now been edited to make sense.



Intended Answers1. 44

2. 24

3. 44 (Probability is  $\frac{17}{27}$ )

4.16

5.528

6.840
